title: Vitamin D, Calcium and Body or Joint Pain: Do You Need Supplements?
metaDescription: Low vitamin D can cause bone pain and weak muscles, but supplements do not fix general aches. Learn what trusted health bodies say about testing and dose.
intro: Not everyone with body or joint pain needs vitamin D or calcium tablets. Low vitamin D can cause bone pain and weak muscles, so a blood test is the way to check. Supplements will not fix general aches, and taking too much can do harm. Ask your doctor about testing and the right dose for you.

sections.heading: What do vitamin D and calcium do for bones?
sections.body: Vitamin D helps the body absorb calcium, and calcium supports bone strength. Muscles and nerves also need vitamin D. Most people make vitamin D when sunlight falls on their skin, and food and supplements add to this.

sections.heading: Can low vitamin D cause bone or body pain?
sections.body: Yes, in some people. Severe lack of vitamin D can cause osteomalacia in teenagers and adults. This is a softening of bones that leads to bone pain and muscle weakness. In children, it can cause rickets, where bones soften and bend. Low vitamin D is also linked to weak, painful muscles. However, many other things cause aches, such as arthritis or strain, so pain alone does not prove you are deficient.

sections.heading: How do I know if my vitamin D is low?
sections.body: A blood test measures vitamin D (called 25-hydroxyvitamin D). The NIH Office of Dietary Supplements says a level of 50 nmol/L or above is adequate for most people. A level below 30 nmol/L is too low and might weaken bones.  Let your doctor interpret the result. Ask your doctor whether testing is right for you.

sections.heading: How much vitamin D is recommended?
sections.body: Recommendations differ by country. The NHS in the UK says adults need 10 micrograms (400 IU) a day. It advises everyone to consider a supplement in autumn and winter, and people at higher risk to take one all year. Higher-risk groups include people who rarely go outdoors, people who cover most of their skin, and people with dark skin. The NIH lists 15 micrograms (600 IU) a day for adults up to age 70 and 20 micrograms (800 IU) from age 71. These are general amounts. If you are deficient, your doctor may prescribe a different dose for a set period.

sections.heading: Can I take too much vitamin D or calcium?
sections.body: Yes. Both the NHS and NIH set an upper limit of 100 micrograms (4,000 IU) a day for adults from all sources. Too much over a long time can build up calcium in the body and harm the kidneys and heart. Very high blood levels can cause nausea, vomiting, muscle weakness and confusion, and excess almost always comes from supplements. For calcium, the NIH upper limit is 2,500 mg a day for ages 19 to 50 and 2,000 mg for ages 51 and above, including food. Calcium tablets can cause gas or constipation and can interfere with some medicines.

sections.heading: Do supplements prevent fractures or ease joint pain?
sections.body: The evidence is limited. The NIH says vitamin D and calcium supplements slightly increase bone strength in older adults, but it is unclear whether they reduce falls or fractures. It does not say they relieve joint pain. Supplements are one part of bone care, along with food, exercise and, where needed, osteoporosis medicines.

sections.heading: What is our usual approach to aches and pains?
sections.body: We look for the cause first, and care is tailored to you. Pain is usually treated with medicines first. Once pain eases, exercise and strengthening help most people. If you have signs of low vitamin D, such as bone pain with muscle weakness, we may suggest a blood test. If you are deficient, we advise a dose with you. Other options are discussed only if still needed, and the choice stays with you.

faqs.q: Should everyone with joint pain take vitamin D?
faqs.a: No. Joint pain has many causes, and supplements are not shown to relieve it. Ask your doctor whether a test is needed.
The NHS says from late March or early April to the end of September, most people in the UK can make enough from sunlight. That advice is for the UK, so ask your doctor what applies to you in India.
The NIH lists milk, yogurt and cheese, canned fish with bones, kale, broccoli and bok choy, and fortified foods.

faqs.q: Can I take vitamin D without a prescription?
faqs.a: The NHS says supplements are available at most pharmacies and supermarkets. Still, check the dose with your doctor, particularly if you take other medicines.

faqs.q: Which medicines interact with vitamin D or calcium?
faqs.a: The NIH lists steroids, statins, orlistat and thiazide diuretics for vitamin D. Calcium can interfere with some thyroid medicine and antibiotics. Tell your doctor what you take.
